newsitem.title: JAPAN: ADB faces mid-life crisis at 30th annual meeting.
newsitem.headline: ADB faces mid-life crisis at 30th annual meeting.

text.p: The Asian Development Bank, entering a mid-life crisis among its economically and politically diverse members, spent the second day of its lavish 30th birthday party listening to all the guests complain.

The 56-member agency, established in 1966 with a simple mission -- to help Asia's poor -- was scolded by some members for its lack of financial savvy and warned by others not to adopt any political agenda.

The bank, seen by many observers as worthy but increasingly ineffective, has made the search for its new role in Asia the main objective at its annual meeting, which began Sunday in a sprawling hotel complex in this southern Japanese city.

Its two biggest challenges are tighter purse strings at its traditional donors, who face their own budgetary constraints, and the need to move on from its traditional lending activities to more sophisticated project financing involving the private sector.
Top shareholders Japan and the United States both noted at the gathering the scarcity of funds from donor nations and called for the more efficient channelling of ADB's money.

The bank's private sector group (PSG), established in 1995 in order to better coordinate with businesses, was told by ADB advisers that it must launch market-oriented financial products and promote them.

"There is a possibility that, unless the PSG's products are aligned to the marketplace, the ADB will be marginalised in its efforts to become a major force in promoting private-sector infrastructure," said a report released on Monday by a joint working group of the ADB and the International Institute of Finance.
It added that the ADB must shift from mere lending to providing risk guarantees.

"I believe that the bank's role will need to evolve from predominantly a financier of development projects...to become more of a catalyst in the development process," Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam said.

Host nation Japan also stressed a more catalytic role for the bank, saying on Sunday that the ADB Institute, scheduled to open in Tokyo later this year, will explore intellectual exchanges and new development philosophies for the 21st century.
But as some pushed the bank to go beyond its traditional lender role, other members fumed that it should stick to its original purpose.

"We are concerned with the declining proportion of contributions from the donors' resources and would like to strongly urge traditional donors to share your wealth," Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said.

Malaysian deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim added, "whilst acknowledging the need to allocate the limited concessionary resources effectively, I would like to urge the bank to ensure that such policies would not result in the marginalisation of the poorer developing countries."
The harshest words came from Burma, which has had its ADB aid suspended for the past decade.
Finance minister Brigadier General Win Tin said the bank was established to provide financial and technical assistance to all member countries without any political influence.
"Moreover, the bank's objective is to give special attention to the needs of the less developed member countries," Win Tin said.
